title: Chief Theodore “Blue Medicine” Green
summary: Theodore “Blue Medicine” Green (1927–2007) was a Setalcott leader and community historian who documented family heritage and helped bring living Setalcott history into public view.
content:
Theodore “Blue Medicine” Green (1927–2007) was a Setalcott leader, historian, and former trustee of the Three Village Historical Society.1

Family history as public history

Green documented Setalcott family heritage in the Christian Avenue community. Columbia University’s Mapping the African American Past places his research within a neighborhood shaped by Native and African American families, including the Harts, Sells, Eatos, and Greens. Family connections are central to this story; one racial label cannot describe every resident’s identity.2

A gathering that made continuity visible

In a 2017 interview, Helen “Hart of Morning Star” Sells credited her cousin Green with founding the Setalcott Corn Festival Pow-Wow in 2005. She described its educational purpose: helping neighbors recognize Native culture and the Setalcott Nation’s continuing place in local history.3

Places connected with his work

Explore the Christian Avenue historic district, Setalcott Powwow Grounds, and Three Village Historical Society. The map connects community and public-history places, not Green’s home or a reconstructed travel route. School grounds are an event venue only when opened for an announced public gathering.

  2. Mapping the African American Past, Setauket, paragraphs on Christian Avenue families and Theodore Green. Columbia University, unpaginated web exhibit.

why_this_matters: Green’s work connects genealogy, community gatherings, and museum interpretation. His story shows how Indigenous people shape the public history of their own communities.
